replying_to: Replying to Iterative Importance Fine-tuning of Diffusion Models
display_title: Official Review of Submission12066 by Reviewer cW2k

summary.value: Oftentimes we want to use a pretrained diffusion model as a prior for conditional sampling for some downstream task. The posterior distribution in this case can be thought of as a tilted version of the pretrained diffusion model's distribution. One method of sampling from such tilted distributions involves using the Doob's h-transform. In this paper, the authors propose an iterative algorithm for estimating the h-transform. Specifically, they propose refining the estimate of the h-transform by sampling from the diffusion model using the current estimate of the h-transform, filtering samples based on how well they fit the tilted distribution, and using those samples for supervised fine-tuning. This procedure is applied iteratively many times, yielding a sequence of improved estimates for the h-transform. They present experiments applying this approach to class-conditional sampling, super-resolution, and reward-based finetuning.

strengths.value: The paper is well-written and presents a novel method for estimating the h-transform to improve conditional sampling from diffusion models, which draws on methods such as importance based fine-tuning as well as iterative fine-tuning procedures. Notably, this method does not require differentiating the score function of the base model and also is more memory efficient than other methods. The authors additionally prove that their iterative approach is a descent algorithm that minimizes the general loss function for the h-transform and that the distribution of samples at each step is closer to that of the tilted distribution.

weaknesses.value:
The experiments in the paper could be improved. For class-conditional sampling, I would like to see additional results in a more difficult setting with more classes such as ImageNet. For super-resolution, I would like to see a few different things. First, I think there should be experiments with more than 2x super-resolution, such as 4x and 8x super-resolution. Additionally, I would like to see experiments on additional datasets, such as ImageNet and CelebA-HQ, which are more standard. For super-resolution, I also don't think you compare with other methods, such as DDRM [1] and SR3 [2]. For reward-based fine-tuning, you should use a larger set of prompts for evaluation. Finally, you should compare with additional baselines. SMC-based approaches also allow for sampling from the tilted distribution and you should compare with recent SMC-based methods for this problem, such as FK Steering [3]. I would also like to see a simple Best-of-N baseline for each setting.

[1] Kawar, Bahjat, Michael Elad, Stefano Ermon, and Jiaming Song. "Denoising diffusion restoration models." NeurIPS 2022. [https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/95504595b6169131b6ed6cd72eb05616-Abstract-Conference.html](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/95504595b6169131b6ed6cd72eb05616-Abstract-Conference.html).

[2] Saharia, Chitwan, Jonathan Ho, William Chan, Tim Salimans, David J. Fleet, and Mohammad Norouzi. "Image super-resolution via iterative refinement." IEEE transactions on pattern analysis and machine intelligence 2022. [https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9887996/](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9887996/).

[3] Singhal, Raghav, Zachary Horvitz, Ryan Teehan, Mengye Ren, Zhou Yu, Kathleen McKeown, and Rajesh Ranganath. "A General Framework for Inference-time Scaling and Steering of Diffusion Models." ICML 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06848](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06848).

comment.value:
Thank you very much for your review and your constructive feedback. Based on your comment, we extended the experimental part by several aspects. We outline the major changes and responses to your detailed comments as follows:

- **Super-resolution experiment**: We stress that the main intention behind this example is to numerically validate the claim from Theorem 6 that the stochastic optimal control loss decreases. We added more baselines for the example: minimization of the stochastic optimal control (SOC) loss from eqt (9) using VarGrad [1], posterior sampling using DPS [2] and Top-K (Best-of-N) sampling. Notice that Top-K (even with $K=64$) does not provide samples, which are consistent to the observations $y^\delta$. 

- **SMC Comparison**: Thank you for the suggestion. We added FK-Steering as a baseline. We refer to the updated Table 4 for the results.

- **Non-differentiable Reward**: Thank you for this suggestion. We added a modified version of the example for class-conditional sampling with a non-differentiable reward, we refer to the new experiment in Section 4.3 in the paper. More precisely, we define the reward $r$ as $r(x)=1$ if the correct class is sampled and $r(x)=0$ otherwise. Such settings could be relevant in practice, if the classifier is not fully accessible. Alternatively, one could also incorporate human feedback without training a reward network. Our results show that importance fine-tuning works similarly as before while most baselines are not applicable. 

- **Top-K Sampling**: We added Top-K (Best-of-N) sampling as a simple baseline to both the super-resolution (see Figure 6) and the non-smooth class conditional example (see Table 2). For the reward fine-tuning experiment we already compared to Top-K in the main paper. 

- **Choice of prompts**: We roughly orientated on the experiments carried out in the RTB paper [3]. 

Finally, we stress that our paper introduces a new methodology, has significant theoretical contributions and already provides a variety of examples including larger image models like stable diffusion and the Flowers dataset. Therefore, we consider further experiments on CelebA-HQ and ImageNet out-of-range for the rebuttal.

[1] Richter et al. "VarGrad: A Low-Variance Gradient Estimator for Variational Inference" (2020)

[2] Chung et al. "Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems" (2022)

[3] Venkatraman et al. "Amortizing intractable inference in diffusion models for vision, language, and control" (Neurips, 2024)

display_title: Official Review of Submission12066 by Reviewer 4U4W

summary.value: This paper presents a new method to finetune diffusion models to achieve high rewards. The main idea is an iterative approach, where the models are continuously trained on importance-weighted samples (or with a similar rejection sampling adjustment). These reweighted samples are supposed to align with the posterior distribution, induced by the prior distribution model and the exponentiated reward. The method is compared to a range of other methods in synthetic 2D, image super-resolution, class-conditional image generation and text-to-image generation tasks.

strengths.value: The paper in general is easy to follow. The proposed idea is simple and straightforward to implement.

weaknesses.value:
The main weakness of the current submission is that the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed method remain unclear. The presentation lacks critical algorithmic details, making it difficult to understand how the method actually work. Moreover, the empirical comparisons to prior work are limited and not convincingly justified. See more details below, 

- Important algorithmic details are not included in the main paper. The choice of hyperparameter $c$ should be important for the efficiency of rejection sampler, however it is not discussed and only reference is mentioned to prior work. Similarly, while the computation of importance weights are built upon prior work, it should be explained in the main paper for the completeness of the method. The importance weights presented in Alg. 13 is not directly tractable.

- Empirical evaluation should include the algorithm efficiency or complexity aspects. For example, how many total training samples each method uses, and what is the sample acceptance rate for the proposed method. If we control for such compute factors, what is the margin of the proposed method to others?

- For each experiment subsection, too few benchmarks are considered. For example, inverse problem in sec 4.2 only includes one example, and text-to-image reward finetuning only includes 3 prompts. In addition,  I believe the paper can benefit from adding more baseline methods for comparison ,for example, for the image super-resolution task. 

- Empirical results did not include standard errors. 

- Finally, as the authors pointed out in the limitation section, such importance sampling or rejection sampling methods rely on the assumption that the proposal (the prior model) has sufficient support on the high reward region. This point is more about the assumption of the method rather than a critique.

questions.value:
- Eq 16 states parameterizes the network with reward gradient conditioning. Is my understanding correct that is reward gradient conditioning is used across all experiments except the text-to-image ones? What would happen if you didn't use such conditioning for the remaining experiments? 

- Why is the Stochastic loss presented in Figure 2? Isn't the proposed method trained on $L_{FT}$ loss in eq 15?

comment.value:
Thank you for reviewing our paper. Before addressing the specific weaknesses and questions you raised, we would like to clarify two key points that are central to our work:

- Our paper considers self-supervised fine-tuning of diffusion models. In particular, as outlined at various places in the paper (e.g., TL;DR, Abstract, Introduction and in Section 3 and 4), **neither the proposed method nor any of the comparisons requires any training samples**. All samples which appear in the supervised fine-tuning loss in eqt (15) are previously **generated by the model itself**.

- The **importance weights from eqt (13) are directly tractable** (up to the time discretization) and **can be computed on the fly** during generating the corresponding sample (by using the same time-discretization for the integrals as for the simulation of the backward SDE). 

Replies to the raised weaknesses and questions


> Important algorithmic details are not included in the main paper. The choice of hyperparameter $c$ should be important for the efficiency of rejection sampler, however it is not discussed and only reference is mentioned to prior work. 

For choosing $c$, we note that by definition the acceptance ratio $\alpha(x_{[0:T]})$ is monotone decreasing in $c$. In particular, it is straightforward to establish a bisection search algorithm which ensures that $\mathbb{E}[\alpha(x_{[0:T]})]=\rho$ for a prescribed acceptance ratio $\rho$, where the expectation is taken over the batch of generated samples. We agree that this adaptive choice of $c$ is important for the algorithm as it ensures that  always a sensible portion of the generated samples is accepted. This ensures that on one side enough samples are accepted to maintain diversity, but on the other side enough samples are rejected to effectively filter the dataset. We extended the explanation how this $c$ can be found in the paper.

> Similarly, while the computation of importance weights are built upon prior work, it should be explained in the main paper for the completeness of the method. The importance weights presented in Alg. 13 is not directly tractable.

We want to stress that the importance weights in Equation (13) can be computed at sampling time with no additional network evaluation, if the integrals are discretised using the same time discretisation as the SDE. Up to the time-discretisation, we use **exactly eqt 13** for computing the importance weights and no additional calculations are needed. Also, we provide a derivation of the RND $\frac{dP_{data}}{dP_h}$ (used in Equation 12) in Appendix A, both for the SDE and the discrete DDPM case. 

> Empirical evaluation should include the algorithm efficiency or complexity aspects. For example, how many total training samples each method uses, and what is the sample acceptance rate for the proposed method. If we control for such compute factors, what is the margin of the proposed method to others?

As outlined in the beginning, neither our algorithm nor the comparisons have access to any training samples. As outlined in the paper, the acceptance rate of the samples can be controlled by the parameter $c$ in eqt (14). We choose $c$ such that a prescribed fraction of the generated samples is accepted. This fraction depends on the experiment and reported in the appendix. For instance, in the text-to-image diffusion example it is choosen as 10%. To give a feeling of the computational effort for each algorithm, we added a table in the appendix (cf. Table 7) which reports the computation time and peak memory for every method. Please note, that this comparison should be interpreted cautiously, as training time and GPU memory can be traded off, for example, via gradient accumulation to increase effective batch size or gradient checkpointing. The different comparison methods implement vary in the use of the techniques.

I would like to thank the authors for their response (both Part I and Part II). 

A couple of follow up questions and comments:

1. The point I made about Eq 13 is intractable is that evaluating the integral exactly is intractable. It appears from the response that this integral is approximated with discretization. 

2. Is my understanding correct that your method only optimizes the loss in Eq 15, i.e. L_{FT}? And the SOC loss and mean loss presented in Figure 2 are for the baseline methods?

3. Can you discuss the impact of using c!=1 in the relaxed rejection sampling in Eq 14? I am not familiar with the cited work, Hertrich & Gruhlke (2025). Is the relaxed rejection sampling still unbiased? If not, what are the implications of this sampling bias in the overall algorithm? 

4. While the authors have justified using reward gradient as a network preconditioning, I feel it can still be a limitation as it slows down the inference speed and creates additional overhead.

comment.value:
> For each experiment subsection, too few benchmarks are considered. For example, inverse problem in sec 4.2 only includes one example, and text-to-image reward finetuning only includes 3 prompts. In addition, I believe the paper can benefit from adding more baseline methods for comparison ,for example, for the image super-resolution task.

Thank you for the suggestions. We uploaded a revised manuscript which contains more benchmarks: For the super-resolution example, we added two baselines: the direct minimization of the stochastic optimal control (SOC) loss from eqt (9) as a baseline and its approximation with the RTB [1] approximation. We run these experiments on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24GB memory. In particular, the direct minimization of the SOC requires backpropagation of the full sampling chain and is only possible by making heavy use of gradient checkpointing and gradient accumulation. In this case a single gradient descent step requires about $30$s, leading to a significantly higher runtime than importance fine-tuning.  

Further, in Appendix D.2 Figure 5 we present additional results for other images from the Flowers test set. In particular, we fine-tune models for the first $5$ images from the test set and present the mean sample and the pointwise standard deviation. In addition, we present in Figure 14 two more prompts for the text-to-image example.

Based on the comments of other reviewers, we added a comparison to FK Steering [2] to the text-to-image example. Finally, we added an example using a non-differentiable reward function in the new Section 4.3. While most of the comparisons are not applicable for this case, our importance fine-tuning works similar as for the differentiable case.

> Empirical results did not include standard errors.

We emphasize that we are dealing with very large models (particularly for the text-to-image examples). Therefore, taking standard errors over several training runs is computationally very demanding. We believe that this is common in this field and note that none of the common baselines (DPOK, RTB, Adjoint Matching, FK Steering) reports standard errors (for the same reason).

> Inductive Bias using the reward gradient 

It is correct, that we used the reward gradient conditioning for all experiments despite the text-to-image example. Not using it results in a slightly larger training time and sometimes also in a slight drop of the performance.

Based on the comment of the other reviewers, we have now added an additional example with a non-differentiable reward function, which also doesn't use the reward gradient (since it does not exists). In particular, most comparisons (like adjoint matching) require differentiable reward functions and are not applicable in this setting, highlighting another advantage of importance fine-tuning.


> Stochastic Loss in Figure 2

We prove in Theorem 6 that the stochastic optimal control loss from eqt (9) is decreased throughout the iterations. The main purpose of the super-resolution example is to numerically validate this result. Also, **reporting the fine-tuning loss (15) does not make any sense** in this context, since it depends on the iteration $k$ through the distribution $\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{h^k}^0$, where the samples are drawn from. In particular, the **loss values of the fine-tuning loss (15) are not comparable over the iterations**.

[1] Venkatraman et al. "Amortizing intractable inference in diffusion models for vision, language, and control" (Neurips, 2024)

[2] Singhal, Raghav, Zachary Horvitz, Ryan Teehan, Mengye Ren, Zhou Yu, Kathleen McKeown, and Rajesh Ranganath. "A General Framework for Inference-time Scaling and Steering of Diffusion Models." ICML 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06848.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission12066 by Reviewer 4U4W

comment.value:
Thank you for your reply!

> The point I made about Eq 13 is intractable is that evaluating the integral exactly is intractable. It appears from the response that this integral is approximated with discretization.

Yes, in particular we discretise the integral using the same time discretisation as the reverse SDE for sampling. We added a comment in the paper that we use a time discretisation. Note, that in Appendix A.1 we provide a version of the importance weights for the time discrete setting (DDPMs).


> Is my understanding correct that your method only optimizes the loss in Eq 15, i.e. L_{FT}? And the SOC loss and mean loss presented in Figure 2 are for the baseline methods?

No, this is not correct. Let us recap the basic functionality of the proposed method as outlined in Section 3. We generate a sequence $(h^k)_k$ of guidance functions by 

1. Sampling with guidance term $h^{k-1}$
2. Filtering with importance weights
3. Retraining with $\mathcal L_{FT}$

**We prove in Theorem 6 that $\mathrm{SOC}(h^k)\leq \mathrm{SOC}(h^{k-1})$.** In that sense, we are **minimising the SOC loss**. But you are right that as intermediate steps we minimise the loss $\mathcal L_{FT}$ and that the minimisation of the SOC loss is implicit in the sense that we **never perform gradient updates on the SOC loss**.

> Can you discuss the impact of using c!=1 in the relaxed rejection sampling in Eq 14? I am not familiar with the cited work, Hertrich & Gruhlke (2025). Is the relaxed rejection sampling still unbiased? If not, what are the implications of this sampling bias in the overall algorithm?

Note that the classical importance weights (up to a normalizing constant) are recovered by the choice $c\geq \max_{x_{[0:T]}}\\{\frac{dP_{data}}{dP_h}(x_{[0:T]})\exp(r(x_0))\\}$, since then the minimum in the definition of $\alpha$ is never applied (the choice $c=1$ does not lead to a meaningful special case). For this choice of $c$, we obtain that the accepted samples exactly follow the tilted distribution (*). However, numerically this leads to vanishing acceptance rates and is therefore numerically unstable. Therefore, we consider smaller (adaptive) choices of $c$, where we obtain an interpolation between the current estimate $P_h$ and $P_\text{tilted}$. In this sense, the relaxed importance weights are not unbiased. The implication is that we have to iterate the procedure (i.e., generate a sequence $(h^k)_k$) and do not obtain the tilted distribution in one step. On the other hand, the relaxation is required to obtain a numerical stable algorithm.

Mathematically spoken, the distributions $\frac{\alpha}{E[\alpha]}P_h$ interpolate between the current estimate $P_h$ and $P_{\text{tilted}}$ in the Fisher-Rao geometry, where $c\to\infty$ yields $P_{\text{tilted}}$ and $c\to 0$ yields the current estimate $P_{h}$.

(*) We guess that this is what you refer as unbiased, since it can equivalently be formulated as $E_{x\sim P_h}[\frac{\alpha(x)}{E_{y\sim P_h}[\alpha(y)]}f(x)]=E_{x\sim P_\text{tilted}} [f(x)]$ for any measurable $f$ (which is the typical unbiasednes property of importance weights).

> While the authors have justified using reward gradient as a network preconditioning, I feel it can still be a limitation as it slows down the inference speed and creates additional overhead.

In our view, this discussion is not specific to our method, but a trade-off which is relevant to any training-based diffusion guidance method. By using the reward gradient as preconditioning, we trade an increase of performance against a drop in the inference speed. 

We emphasize that we neither invented nor modified this preconditioning. In our paper we demonstrate that we can use it and that we can reproduce the performance increase, but that our method also works without it (both observations are consistent with the literature). But the general discussion of its advantages and disadvantages is a bit orthogonal to our contributions.

summary.value:
Given a diffusion model $p_\theta(x_0)$ and a reward model $r(x_0)$, the authors propose a method to sample from the reward tilted distribution. The authors introduce a fine-tuning method that builds on the h-transform learning framework introduced in Denker et al 2024, which learns the gradient of the intermediate reward $\nabla_{x_t} \log E_{p(x_0 | x_t)}[\exp(r(x_0))]$. 

- Unlike typical fine-tuning (or equivalently variational inference) methods that make use of the reverse KL, the authors propose using the supervised, forward KL, objective in eq 7.
- However, as samples from the tilted distribution are not available, the authors use the current iteration of the fine-tuned model to generate samples and then defining an accept/reject step using the Radon-Nikodym derivative (ie the importance weight) between the tilted path measure and the model defined path measure.

strengths.value: Unlike prior methods such as RAFT that make use of importance sampling with the current iteration as the proposal generator, the authors derive a principled approach for fine-tuning. The authors propose a tractable accept/reject probability for use in the diffusion fine-tuning setting.

weaknesses.value:
1. The authors should engage with existing literature in a more thorough manner. For instance, iterative cross-entropy (De Boer et al 2005), reinforced self-training (Gulcehre et al 2023), and RAFT (Dong et al 2023), all use importance-sampling and rejection sampling for fine-tuning.
2. As baselines, the authors should include a comparison to sequential Monte Carlo methods, which in the low particle regime have been shown to outperform fine-tuned models. 
3. The authors also make use of reward gradient in parameterizing the h-transform, making it unclear to what extent the proposed fine-tuning method works.

De Boer, Pieter-Tjerk, et al. "A tutorial on the cross-entropy method." Annals of operations research 134.1 (2005): 19-67.

Gulcehre, Caglar, et al. "Reinforced self-training (rest) for language modeling." arXiv preprint arXiv:2308.08998 (2023).

Dong, Hanze, et al. "Raft: Reward ranked finetuning for generative foundation model alignment." arXiv preprint arXiv:2304.06767 (2023).

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission12066 by Reviewer q1ny

comment.value:
**1. Related Work** 

Thank you for the suggestion of additional related work. We agree that we agree that the proposed importance fine-tuning algorithm belongs to the family of cross-entropy methods and added a note to the explanation of our approach in Section 3.2. 

Regarding RAFT and REST: While we have already cited RAFT in our paper, we have now extended the explanations on it in the related works section. As part of that we now explain that REST and RAFT can be viewed as the limit case $\lambda^{-1}\to\infty$ of importance fine-tuning. In this limit, the relevance of the Radon-Nikodym derivative within the importance weights vanishes such that only the reward remains, and we choose the accepted trajectories only based on the reward. 

In particular, RAFT and REST perform filtering based solely on the reward value. In contrast, our method leverages the full importance weights, which incorporate both the reward and the divergence between the current and initial models (i.e., the Radon–Nikodym derivative $\frac{dP_{data}}{dP_{h}}$). As shown in Figure 1, using only the reward for weighting or filtering trajectories can cause mode collapse. This phenomenon is also analysed theoretically in [4], where Theorem 2.1 demonstrates that the limiting distribution in such cases is not the tilted distribution $p_\text{data}(x) \exp(r(x)/\lambda)$, but rather the initial distribution restricted to the region that maximizes the reward.

Further, in the Stable Diffusion experiments we compare to the case $\lambda^{-1} = \infty$, which recovers the setting in RAFT, i.e., choosing the trajectories only based on the reward value. We added a discussion to this in the experimental section.



**2. Additional comparison** 

Thank you for the suggestion to compare with SMC-based methods. Following the suggestion of Reviewer cW2k, we added a comparison against FK-Steering [2] for the reward fine-tuning experiment. We followed the same configuration as reported in [2] based on the source code of [2]. To obtain 100 independent samples, we executed 100 independent FK-Steering runs, each with $k$ particles, and selected one final particle at random from each run.

For $k = 4$ particles (the suggested value from [2]), we found that the effective sample size (ESS) for FK-Steering was typically close to 1. Therefore, all $4$ particles from a single execution looked very similar and the results were below our Top-K sampling for $k=6$, (which is consistent with the findings of other papers, see, e.g., [3]). Therefore used $k=6$ for the comparison in the paper. For the detailed results, see the table below and Table 4 in the paper.


| Method | Metric | "A green colored rabbit" | "Two roses in a vase" | "Two dogs in the park" |
| -------- | -------- | -------- |-------- |-------- |
| FK-Steering (k=4)    | Reward     | $0.944$     | $1.592$     | $0.922$     |
| FK-Steering (k=4)    | Diversity     | $0.162$     | $0.109$     | $0.157$     |
| FK-Steering (k=6)    | Reward     | $1.207$   | $1.645$  |  $0.985$   |
| FK-Steering (k=6)    | Diversity     |  $0.147$   | $0.108$  | $0.139$   |
| Top-K (k=6)     | Reward     | $1.334$     | $1.619$     | $0.970$     |
| Top-K (k=6)     | Diversity     | $0.149$     | $0.121$     | $0.161$     |
| Importance FT (ours)     | Reward     | $1.462$     | $1.524$     | $1.010$     |
| Importance FT (ours)     | Diversity     | $0.051$     | $0.077$     | $0.120$     |

display_title: Inductive Bias with the reward gradient

title.value: Inductive Bias with the reward gradient

comment.value:
**3. Inductive Bias with the reward gradient** 

Reward gradients are widely used as inductive bias for sampling and fine-tuning methods and we would not consider it as a general weakness (even though we agree that it has some limitations). We emphasize two points:

- We **don't use it for all experiments**. As outlined in Section 3.3, we do not use reward gradients for the Stable Diffusion example. Indeed this also would not be practical, since computing the reward gradients can be quite costly in this case. Instead it uses a LoRA parameterization which reduces the cost of the fine-tuning network.

- Generally, using reward gradients as inductive bias **is not required for importance fine-tuning**, in contrast to plenty other sampling and fine-tuning methods, see, e.g., [1]. Nevertheless, we observe that it reudces the training time and slightly improves the results.

Following the suggestion of Reviewer cW2k, we **added an additional experiment using a piecewise constant reward function**. Here, the reward gradient carries no useful signal, the inductive bias for the network architecture cannot be applied. In particular, the added Table 2 compares the results on the MNIST example with smooth reward (and reward gradients) and non-smooth reward (without using reward gradients). We observe that our method still works under these conditions and only drops slighly in the performance.


[1] He et al. "No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers" (2025)

[2] Singhal et al. "A General Framework for Inference-time Scaling and Steering of Diffusion Models" (2025)

[3] Anonoymus "Scaling Atomistic Protein Binder Design with Generative Pretraining and Test-Time Compute" (current ICLR submission: https://openreview.net/forum?id=qmCpJtFZra)

[4] Ferbach et al. "Self-consuming generative models with curated data provably optimize human preferences." (2024)

summary.value: This work tackles the problem of fine-tuning a diffusion model $p_\theta(x_0)$ to sample from the reward-tilted distribution $p_{\mathrm{tilted}}(x) \propto p_\theta(x_0) \exp(r(x_0))$. It does so by obtaining approximate samples from $p_{\mathrm{tilted}}(x)$, and then minimizing the denoising score matching loss on these samples. The approximate samples are obtained by sampling from the model in its current iteration, and correcting them using a rejection sampling scheme with importance weights computed over trajectories. This optimization algorithm (with importance sampling) is shown to monotonically minimize the reverse KL ($KL(p_{\theta}(x) || p_{\mathrm{tilted}}(x))$ to the target distribution. The method is demonstrated by reward-tilted sampling for 2D Gaussian mixture models, class conditional sampling in MNIST, a linear-inverse problem in super-resolution, and improving prompt alignment in Stable Diffusion.

strengths.value:
1. The main important contribution of the paper is the use of relaxed importance sampling (from (Hertrich & Gruhlke, 2025)) to bypass the requirement of a fine-tuning dataset (as in DEFT), which is a useful and important improvement over that algorithm
    - Theorem 6, and the empirical validation in Fig 2 is useful for demonstrating that the relaxed importance sampling method doesn’t compromise theoretical validity of the method.
2. The method has a benefit over other methods in not storing (or backpropagating through) trajectories for training
3. The experimental settings chosen are relevant and useful for the proposed method (class conditional sampling, inverse problems, and prompt-alignment)
    - The method is demonstrated on a larger scale problem in prompt alignment for Stable Diffusion
4. The work is clearly written and has a logical presentation of ideas

weaknesses.value:
1) The use of the replay buffer requires further explanation or justification, since it is critical to the efficiency of the algorithm:
    - Why is it reasonable to use a replay buffer? Shouldn’t trajectories be drawn on-policy (according to current $h$ ) to have the correct importance weights computed according to eq. 14 (I am assuming the accepted samples are placed in the buffer, as described in Algorithm 1)?
        - Notably in other works (eg. in Sendera et. al., 2024), the use of a replay buffer is justified by the training loss itself not needing on-policy samples, but such a justification doesn’t seem to hold for the proposed algorithm
        - Is there any degradation in performance for longer buffer lengths, it would be helpful to experimentally demonstrate the impact of the replay buffer.
        

2) For experiments - some more comprehensive evaluations are needed to demonstrate the performance of the method:
    - For the toy GMM task - from the figure or the reported metrics in Table 4 it is unclear whether the proposed method is less biased compared to alternatives (in particular classifier guidance). A metric based on reverse KL, or a comparison to a “ground truth” baseline (such as a diffusion model trained on ground truth samples from $p_{\mathrm{tilted}}$) would better illustrate the performance
    - For the linear inverse problem - the method should be compared to baselines such as VarGrad, or Adjoint Matching, to demonstrate how the method compares to alternatives
    - For prompt alignment fine-tuning - the images  produced by Importance FT seem overly bright and saturated, or with some artefacts, compared to the other fine-tuning methods (in Fig 4, as well as 8, 9, 10). Is there any degradation in performance due to the fine-tuning?

3) The advantages for the proposed method should be more clearly outlined, over the alternatives, in particular since the metrics in Table 3 doesn’t show a clear improvement for Importance FT over the alternatives. In my opinion this would be remedied by more empirical support for two claims made in the paper:
    - The conclusion implies the training method is more stable in terms of requiring fewer tricks (eg. loss clipping). Does this hold more broadly?  Eg. does the reward improve more smoothly along training iterations, or do the gradients have smaller variance compared to other baselines? Does the reward improve at a faster rate (either in terms of wall-clock time or the number of gradient updates made)? If so, the method would be more clearly useful.
    - The method has the same memory complexity as Adjoint matching (or other online RL methods using the adjoint method) (O(B)), so the claim of importance FT offering “a more efficient and scalable training pipeline” should be supported more clearly. If there is a time-overhead in adjoint matching compared to Importance FT, its significance to the prompt alignment experiment should be demonstrated clearly.

4) Minor grammar errors include:
   - Line 41 space between citation and “.Further, the tilted …”
   - Between Line 71, 73, “stable diffusion” should be capitalized for consistency
   - Line 179 “… sampling from unnormalised probability density function**s**” (s missing)
   - Line 205 “are in particular satisfied **if** the guidance $h$ …”
   - Line 277 (ii) - Should be “ $\mathbb{P}\_{tilted}$  rather than $\mathbb{P}_{tilde}$” - also proportion sign here doesn’t make sense, it should be off by a constant term
   - Line 400-401: “samples are **shown**”
   - Line 415: “samples **do** not always”
   - Line 473-474: missing word “We present **experiments** for class conditional sampling,”
   - Line 481 quotations around “good” are inverted
   - Line 483 “and high reward samples are are”

5) For related works, the paper is missing a reference and discussions to Particle Denoising Diffusion sampling (Phillips et. al., 2024), which uses a similar optimization scheme of sampling from the current iteration of the model, correcting with importance weights (in their case SMC), and then performing supervised training (albeit targeted at the sampling problem rather than reward fine-tuning).

For now I am recommending a weak accept. The primary concern being point 3 above. If more comprehensive evidence is provided which clearly shows the advantages of the proposed method, then I will strongly consider raising my score.

A. Phillips, H.-D. Dau, M. J. Hutchinson, V. De Bortoli, G. Deligiannidis, and A. Doucet, “Particle denoising diffusion sampler,” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2024.

comment.value:
Thank you very much for the detailed and thoughtful review. We answered each of the raised weaknesses and questions separately.

**1. Usage of replay buffer**

Thank you for pointing this out. The use of replay buffers can be justified if we slightly modify it: Whenever the buffer size is reached, we have to remove samples. If we remove them randomly instead of removing the oldest ones, we can exploit the convexity of the stochastic optimal control (SOC) loss $\mathcal F$ (in the linear space of measures) in order to show that it still decreases over the iterations. However, we observed numerically that removing the oldest samples from the buffer yields very similar results, but converges faster. Therefore, we used this variant during the numerical examples. We extended the explanations on this part and added Appendix C, which explains this point.




**2. Experiments** 

- **toy example GMM**: We already compute the energy distance for this example, which is based on ground truth samples, which is informative in low-dimensions. Further, metrics based on the reverse KL would require the density of the (guided) score model, which is not given in closed form and would need to be estimated. 

- **super-resolution**: We added a comparison against optimising the SOC with VarGrad, DPS and Top-K sampling. For VarGrad, we also computed the final SOC loss and added the result to Figure 2. We compare the samples achived by the different methods in Figure 6. Top-K (even with $K=64$) fails for this example, as it is highley unlikely to draw an image that is consistent with the observations $y^\delta$ by change. 

- **reward fine-tuning**: A key difference between our method and RL-based approaches (such as DPOK or Adjoint Matching) is how classifier-free guidance (CFG) is handled during training. RL methods typically optimize the guided model directly, i.e., they treat $\epsilon_\theta =w \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t,c)+(1-w)\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ with a fixed $w$ for optimisation and use exactly this model at sampling time. Our method instead optimizes a score-matching loss, for which we follow the standard CFG training procedure: the prompt $c$ is randomly dropped during training, and the guided CFG model is constructed only at inference time. This means we do not directly train the **exact** CFG combination used at sampling time and have to choose the guidance scale $w$ at inference time. To be consistent to the other methods, we **did not tune the guidance scale** and choose a fixed guidance scale. However, we can vary the guidance scale and we observe that for smaller guidance scales ($w \approx 4.0$) the saturation artefacts decrease. We added a comparison to the Appendix of the paper, see Figure 13. 


**3. Fix grammatical errors** 

Thank you for pointing this out! This has been fixed in the updated version. 

**4. Discussion of related work**

Thanks for pointing us to this paper. We added it to the related work. Note, that we already cited similar self-supervised methods for sampling from unnormalised densities. In particular, iDEM (Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024) and FAB  (Midgley et al., 2023).

comment.value:
## Advantages of Importance FT over alternative approaches

We now provide a more explicit discussion:

**Non-smooth reward function**: Recent (SOTA) fine-tuning approaches like Adjoint Matching [1] crucially rely on the gradient of the reward to work. Further, other inference-time approaches, e.g. DPS [2] also rely on the gradient of the reward for guidance. Instead, we do not rely on a smooth reward function. To demonstrate this, we repeat the MNIST class conditional sampling experiment. However, instead of using the log-class probs. as the reward, we are only using the class predictions, i.e,
$$r(x) = 
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } c = \arg\max_{c'} \log p(c'|x) \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$
As this reward is piecewise constant, the gradients will be zero almost everywhere. Such scenarios might appear in practical applications, if the classifier (or reward) is a blackbox model, we do not have access to its source, or is too large to efficiently backpropagate through it. We added this experiment to Section 4.3, where we observe that Importance FT is still able to successfully fine-tune the model. However, if the reward is smooth and the gradient is informative, we can make use of it with the reward-informed inductive bias (discussed in Section 3.3). 

**Sampling speed at inference time** Methods that rely on filtering techniques during inference time, like SMC-based sampling (e.g., FK-Steering) or Best-of-K sampling, increase inference-time compute costs. Instead, approaches that fine-tune the model (as the approach we present) have the same compute costs at inference time. Moreover, our approach is complementary to these methods: one can first fine-tune with Importance FT and subsequently use SMC-based approaches at inference-time. We note, however, that this is an advantage of all fine-tuning methods and not specific to our approach.

**Memory Usage/Computational Efficiency** Our approach has the same overall memory complexity (i.e., O(B)) as adjoint matching or DPOK [5]. However, Adjoint Matching requires constructing the adjoint state, which involves backpropagating through the pre-trained model (see Equations 37–39 in [1]), and DPOK constructs a policy gradient for each gradient update. While neither method backpropagates through the full trajectory, the gradient still depends on the entire trajectory, increasing computational overhead. In practice, under default settings (Appendix D.2), Adjoint Matching and DPOK require >30 GB of GPU memory, whereas Importance FT achieves comparable performance with lower memory usage (about 16 GB). We note that direct comparisons of training time or GPU usage are complicated by implementation-specific methods such as gradient checkpointing, gradient accumulation, and low-precision training, which can be used to trade-off GPU memory and training time. 

**Score Matching Loss** A key advantage of methods fine-tuned with a score-matching loss (Theorem 1, (ii)), such as Importance FT or RAFT [6], is computational efficiency. The score-matching loss does not depend on the specific trajectory, but only on the final sample. This also makes it easier to integrate additional ground truth data. If an additional dataset of ground truth data from the tilted distribution is available, we can use both the accepted samples and the ground truth samples in the score-matching fine-tuning loss in Equation (15). Importantly, unlike RAFT, which selects updates based only on raw rewards, we can prove that our approach indeed minimizes a loss function whose global minimum is the exact $h$-transform.

**In summary**, we think that the specific combination of these approaches, i.e., (i) dealing with non-smooth rewards, (ii) same sampling speed at inference time and (iii) computational efficiency by using a score matching loss, in addition with the theoretical guarantees in Theorem 6 is unique to our approach, justifing it as another tool for fine-tuning diffusion models. 

Further, we want to note that all of the aforementioned approaches are not mutually exclusive. One can first use our approach as a initial fine-tuning, than switch to a policy gradient method and finally use SMC-based approaches during inference time.

[1] Domingo-Enrich et al. "Adjoint Matching: Fine-tuning Flow and Diffusion Generative Models with Memoryless Stochastic Optimal Control" (2025)

[2] Chung et al. "Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems" (2022)

[4] Singhal et al. "A General Framework for Inference-time Scaling and Steering of Diffusion Models" (2025)

[5] Fan et al. "DPOK: Reinforcement Learning for Fine-tuning Text-to-Image Diffusion Models" (2023)

[6] Dong et al. "RAFT: Reward ranked finetuning for generative foundation model alignment" (2023)

[7] Venkatraman et al. "Amortizing intractable inference in diffusion models for vision, language, and control" (2024)

[8] Richter et al. "VarGrad: A Low-Variance Gradient Estimator for Variational Inference" (2020)

**Answer to questions:**

*For the classifier guidance used for the 2D GMM, and MNIST - was DPS used, or was a time-conditioned classifier trained?*

We did not train a time-conditioned classifier but instead used DPS. We also tried just using the noisy sample directly and got similar results.

*The main gap in performance for adjoint matching appears to be from moving to a LoRA parameterization. Is there any understanding for why this impacts the method so much?* 

We think the most likely issue is that adjoint matching also changes the noise schedule during fine-tuning (see the last paragraph of Section 4.2 in [1]). That forces the fine-tuned model to both optimise the reward and adjust to the new noise schedule. It seems that the LoRA parametrisation is not flexible enough to adapt well to the new noise schedule. 

*How crucial is the relaxed importance sampling step - eg. if you resampled directly based on the importance weights - what would the effective sample size be? Or would it be infeasible?*

The relaxed importance weights are crucial and the proposed method does not work without it. The effective sample size of the importance weights (without the relaxation) is numerically often very close to 1. The relaxation lower-bounds it by the prescribed acceptance rate times the batch size. In this regard, the relaxed importance weights enforce the method to maintain diversity.

The poor balancing of the importance weights (without relaxation) is a common problem when working with high-dimensional peaky distributions and was observed in many papers, such that methods like annealing or relaxation were developed.

*Given that rejection sampling is used - do you sample a fixed number of trajectories in the outer loop, then accept a portion depending on the weights (to put in the buffer), or do you keep sampling until a fixed number of trajectories is accepted?*

We sample a fixed number of trajectories in the outer loop and put the accepted ones in the buffer. Note, that the acceptance probabilities in Equation (14) contain a hyperparameter $c$, which can be tuned to accept a specific fraction of the trajectories. This can be chosen according to prior knowledge, i.e., for class conditional sampling for MNIST one might choose such that $10\%$ of the trajectories are initially accepted. 

*The claim in Line 72-74 is inaccurate (or unclear) since the method requires running the generation process to obtain trajectories (and importance weights). Did this mean to emphasize that the method doesn’t backpropagate at the level of the trajectory?* 

Exactly, we do not backpropagate at the level of the trajetory. To be more precise: we only ever have to keep a single forward pass of the network in memory. We specified this in the manuscript.

*Why is DPOK memory listed as O(B) instead of O(BT)? The (on-policy) gradient update in that paper appears to require backpropagation at each step of the generation trajectory.*

DPOK uses REINFORCE and additionally drops cross terms in the computation of the gradient for the KL regularisation (Appendix A.3 and Equation (9) in DPOK), this reduces the memory cost from $O(BT)$ to $O(B)$. It still requires backpropagation at each step of the trajectory, but only the current step needs to be kept im memory and the gradient can be accumulated.


*This line (431) is inconsistent with the table “Importance fine-tuning reaches a competitive reward with similar diversity and the same O(B) memory footprint as DPOK or RTB”*

Thank you for pointing this out, it was meant to the "competitive reward to DPOK and RTB" with "same memory footprint as DPOK" and "less than RTB"

Following the recommendations of the conference, we would like to give a short summary for the AC of the rebuttal process.

**Reviewer gj6W** positively commented on major parts of our paper. In the weaknesses section, they stated as their main concern (point 3) that we should outline more clearly the advantages of the proposed method over the comparisons. In response, we now emphasize that importance fine-tuning (i) can deal with non-smooth rewards, (ii) has the same sampling speed at inference time and (iii) is computational efficient by using a score matching loss (iv) has stronger theoretical guarantees (Thm 6) than the comparisons. The reviewer had plenty of additional comments, which we addressed and incorporated in our revised paper.

**Reviewer q1ny** recommended additional literature, asked for an additional comparison and for a clarification regarding the reward gradients as implicit bias. All of these were minor fixes, which we implemented in the revised paper.

For **Reviewer 4U4W** we had the impression that they misunderstood the setting of the considered task. In particular, we clarified that neither the proposed method nor any of the comparisons has access to training data and explained more in detail that the path-based importance weights can directly be computed during sampling via the same time discretization used for the SDE. Moreover, we revisited the implications of our Thm 6, stating that importance fine-tuning minimizes the stochastic optimal control loss, even though we never compute gradients of it. In the revised paper, we added comments for clarification. The reviewer also asked for additional experiments, baselines and evalutations, which we implemented accordingly.

**Reviewer cW2k** positively commented on the methodological part of the paper, but asked for additional experiments. In response, we followed many of their suggestions (comparison to FK Steering, using non-differentiable rewards, additional prompts and additional images and a baseline for super-resolution) and extended the experimental part of the paper accordingly.
